I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
control eating strictly to feel in control

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access' conflicts with the other memory items. Being able to talk about the rape very easily is hard to reconcile with a profile centered on fragmented, unreal, image-based trauma memory and severe PTSD symptoms.

issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Story Feels Unreal' and 'Snapshot Memory' suggest poorly elaborated, emotionally overwhelming trauma memory, which clashes with 'Verbal Access'. This makes the Memory node internally inconsistent.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability' is less coherent with the rest of the profile because the dominant appraisals are global loss and mistrust, while the reported threat pattern is generalized anticipatory danger rather than fear specifically tied to bodily injury. For rape it is possible, but here it is the least well integrated appraisal relative to the other selected items.

vignette:
Sofia sits in the waiting room, a space she knows well from her own work in social ministry, though she has never been on this side of the desk. At forty-seven, she feels a profound disconnect from the woman she was just eight months ago. The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. She had stayed late at the community center, waiting for a parishioner who was delayed, and decided to walk the few blocks home as dusk settled. The walk was usually quiet, a time for her to decompress. That quietness was the first thing he took from her. The silence of the empty side street was absolute for a moment before he grabbed her, a void of sound that felt like the world holding its breath. Now, any unusual silence—a lull in conversation at work, the moment after the furnace clicks off at home—sends a jolt of pure terror through her. She is certain that something violent is about to fill the void.

Her memory of the event is not a continuous story. It exists in her mind as a series of stark, still images, like horrific photographs she cannot discard. There is the snapshot of the cracked pavement beneath her cheek, the glint of his silver watch, the specific floral pattern on the discarded mattress in the alley. When she tries to speak about it, to her husband or now to the intake coordinator, the words jam in her throat. She knows the sequence, but language fails her; all she has are the pictures. And with the pictures comes a wave of guilt so powerful it makes her nauseous. She feels it as a physical weight, a certainty that she is somehow to blame for the delay that put her on that street at that exact time.

This sense of pervasive threat has rewired her daily life. Her husband, Miguel, will text that he is running fifteen minutes late, and for Sofia, that delay is not an inconvenience but a confirmation of catastrophe. In those fifteen minutes, she has already pictured a car crash, a heart attack, a mugging. She cannot relax, not even in her own living room with the doors locked. The state of being at ease feels like a dangerous indulgence, an invitation for disaster to strike when her guard is down. She finds herself constantly scanning, listening, waiting for the other shoe to drop. The woman who once led prayer groups with a calm, open heart now feels like a soldier on enemy territory, twenty-four hours a day.

In the months since the attack, she has come to believe that the joyful, faithful person she once was is gone forever, replaced by this miserable, fearful stranger. Her faith, the bedrock of her life and career, has crumbled. She looks at the crucifix in her office and feels nothing but a hollow ache. How could a benevolent God allow such a thing? This loss has made her work unbearable. She counsels people on finding hope while she herself feels that all faith in humanity is a fool’s errand.

To cope with the chaos inside, she has seized on the few things she can still command. Control has become her obsession. She restricts her eating with rigid precision, weighing every portion, counting every calorie. The feeling of hunger is a sharp, clean distraction; the control over her own plate is a small island of order in a world of violent unpredictability. She feels deeply ashamed of her body, seeing it not as her own but as a scene of a crime. She tells herself, in the quiet moments of self-loathing, that she deserves to suffer, that this constant misery is a fitting punishment. The avoidance of relaxation, the strict diets, the self-recrimination—they have become a form of penance. It was a recent moment at work, when a grieving mother reached for her hand and Sofia flinched away, unable to bear the quiet intimacy of offering comfort, that she knew she could not go on like this. She is here today not with hope, which feels too extravagant, but with a desperate need to stop the freefall, to find a way to exist in the world without being in a constant state of terror.
